candidateRows: Atheism lacks a successful argument establishing that God does not exist.
This is one of Craig's two announced principal contentions and establishes the burden he expects the opposing side to meet.
After limiting the debate to God's existence, Craig introduces his first main contention before turning to his positive arguments for theism.
The universe began to exist and therefore has a transcendent personal cause.
The argument supplies a direct positive inference from a finite cosmic past to a personal creator and anchors Craig's cumulative case.
Craig combines philosophical objections to an actually infinite past with Big Bang cosmology, then characterizes the universe's cause as timeless, immaterial, powerful, and personal.
Cosmic fine-tuning is best explained by intelligent design rather than necessity or chance.
Fine-tuning is a major independent pillar of the positive theistic case and directly supports an intelligent designer of the cosmos.
Craig describes life-permitting constants and initial conditions, rejects physical necessity, argues chance and multiverse accounts are improbable, and infers design.
Objective moral values exist, and their existence entails that God exists.
The moral argument is a distinct principal component of Craig's cumulative case, linking moral objectivity directly to divine existence.
Craig argues that atheistic evolution cannot ground binding moral facts, appeals to moral experience as awareness of real goods and evils, and infers God.
The best explanation of the central historical facts about Jesus is his resurrection, which entails God's existence.
The resurrection argument is essential to the specifically Christian dimension of Craig's case rather than merely generic creator theism.
Craig cites the empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and the disciples' transformed belief, rejects naturalistic explanations, and concludes that Jesus rose.
Immediate experience of God can properly ground knowledge of God's existence without inferential argument.
This provides Craig's cumulative case with a non-inferential epistemic basis for theism independent of the four preceding arguments.
Craig compares belief in God to other properly basic beliefs, argues that such beliefs can be grounded in experience, and urges sincere attention to divine experience.
Religious evidentialism collapses into an unfalsifiable practice of retrospectively fitting scientific discoveries into divine design.
The critique attacks the evidential method underlying the positive design case by arguing that it accommodates every possible scientific outcome.
Craig's earlier presentation of cosmology and fine-tuning as empirical evidence supporting purposeful divine design.
Hitchens contrasts presuppositional and evidential apologetics, invokes the displacement of Paley-style design by evolution, and argues that retrofitted design claims evade falsification.
The waste, extinction, randomness, and suffering in evolutionary history undermine the claim that humanity was the intended product of divine design.
This is Hitchens's substantive counterargument to purposeful fine-tuning, using evolutionary history to challenge benevolent anthropocentric design.
Craig's contention that life-permitting cosmic conditions are best explained by an intelligent designer of the cosmos.
Hitchens highlights mass extinction, humanity's near extinction, evolutionary contingency, and vast biological waste as evidence against a deliberate process centered on human faith.
Atheism need not prove God's nonexistence; it maintains that no convincing evidence requires the divine hypothesis.
The move directly reframes the debate's central burden and states the con side's governing position on whether belief in God is warranted.
Craig's earlier demand that Hitchens supply a successful argument proving atheism and tear down the positive theistic case.
Hitchens disputes Craig's characterization of atheists, distinguishes his position from categorical disproof, and argues that observable phenomena remain explicable without positing God.
Even granting a cosmic creator would not establish a caring, intervening, revelatory, or specifically Christian God.
This directly challenges the inferential bridge from cosmological creation to the personal and interventionist deity required by Christian theism.
After defining his nonbelief, Hitchens distinguishes a possible originating entity from a deity that cares about human conduct, revelation, salvation, prayer, and miracles.
Craig's stated priority of inner spiritual assurance over contrary argument makes his apologetic fundamentally faith-based rather than evidential.
The move attacks the epistemic credibility of Craig's cumulative case by arguing that its conclusions are insulated from potentially defeating evidence.
Craig's presentation of arguments and evidence as rational support for Christian belief.
Hitchens discusses Craig's account of spiritual witness, argues that evidence is subordinated to antecedent commitment, and connects this practice to human pattern-seeking.
Fine-tuning is an inference from severe uncertainty, while cosmic waste, destruction, and eventual extinction count against competent benevolent design.
This is Hitchens's sustained direct answer to one of Craig's principal arguments for God and contests both its evidential basis and design interpretation.
Craig's claim that the universe's life-permitting conditions are best explained by intelligent fine-tuning.
Hitchens stresses limited cosmological knowledge, raises regress and pre-existing-material questions, and cites failed structures and cosmic decay as contrary to purposeful design.
Hitchens supplies no positive argument for atheism, so his lack of belief supports at most agnosticism rather than the nonexistence of God.
The move frames the debate's burden of proof and supports Craig's first overarching contention that no adequate case for atheism has been presented.
Hitchens's account of atheism as lacking sufficient reason to adopt the God hypothesis.
At the outset of his rebuttal, Craig treats Hitchens's refusal to assert disproof as a concession and argues that this posture leaves uncertainty rather than atheism.
Evolution is compatible with Christian theism, and its extreme improbability may itself support divine superintendence rather than atheistic naturalism.
This answers Hitchens's appeal to evolutionary history against design while converting the same subject into affirmative support for divine guidance.
Hitchens's use of evolutionary development, waste, and natural selection to undermine purposeful divine design.
Craig separates scriptural interpretation from scientific doubts, invokes nonliteral Genesis readings, and argues that improbable biological development fits theism better than naturalism.
Craig's arguments form a probabilistic cumulative case for Christian theism, with public deductive arguments complementing personal spiritual knowledge.
The passage defines the standard and structure of Craig's entire affirmative case while directly answering objections about certainty and spiritual witness.
Hitchens's claims that Craig must prove Christianity with certainty and subordinates evidence to spiritual conviction.
Craig clarifies the relation between deism and theism, rejects a certainty requirement, distinguishes personal knowledge from public demonstration, and challenges disputed premises.
Observed fine-tuning remains scientifically robust, and the universe's eventual decay does not show that it was undesigned or purposeless.
This defends one of Craig's principal affirmative arguments by addressing the two major objections Hitchens had just directed against cosmic design.
Hitchens's arguments that fine-tuning rests on uncertainty and is contradicted by cosmic destruction and eventual nothingness.
Craig appeals to scientific recognition of fine-tuning, separates finite duration from absence of design, and says Christian resurrection hope defeats the assumed finality of extinction.
Atheism need not prove a competing worldview; it is the justified rejection of an unsupported supernatural hypothesis that explanatory inquiry does not require.
This directly contests Craig's burden-of-proof framing and supplies Hitchens's governing account of what atheism asserts in the debate.
Craig's contention that absence of a positive disproof of God leaves Hitchens with agnosticism rather than atheism.
Hitchens compares disbelief in God with rejection of other unsupported entities, denies neutrality is required, and maintains that observable processes need no supernatural assumption.
Humanity's long suffering before Christianity and the religion's late, uneven, conflicting transmission undermine claims of benevolent providential design and redemption.
The move uses suffering and unequal access to revelation against both divine benevolence and Craig's specifically Christian account of providential history.
Craig's defense that divine resources remove concerns about waste and that Christ arrived at a providentially optimal historical time.
Hitchens contrasts vast prehistoric misery with a late intervention, then emphasizes unreached populations and incompatible missionary messages before criticizing retrospective accommodations.
Human moral capacities arise from social solidarity and long predate monotheism, while religious sanction adds no unique moral good and enables distinctive harms.
This is Hitchens's principal answer to Craig's moral argument, disputing both the necessity and the beneficial contribution of supernatural moral grounding.
Craig's argument that objective moral values and duties require a transcendent foundation in God.
Hitchens argues believers have no exclusive moral actions, contrasts that with religiously motivated wrongdoing, and grounds durable norms in evolved mutual dependence and society.
Atheism is not a positive belief system but the rejection of an unsupported proposition that people should worship a god.
This definition determines what evidential burden Hitchens accepts and directly shapes the debate over whether atheism itself requires a positive proof.
Craig's challenge that Hitchens's non-theism ambiguously combines atheism, agnosticism, and verificationism.
During Craig's cross-examination, Hitchens rejects the characterization of atheism as a system and instead frames it as living without an inadequately supported divine assumption.
Claims of divine authority require exceptionally strong evidence because they empower other people to command conduct in God's name.
The move supplies Hitchens's evidential standard for theism and connects insufficient evidence to the practical danger of asserted religious authority.
Craig's contention that absence of evidence is not evidence of God's absence and that Hitchens lacks a positive case.
After Craig questions whether missing evidence supports nonexistence, Hitchens distinguishes God from trivial hypothetical entities and stresses the enormous stakes of the claim.
The moral argument concerns an objective foundation for moral duties, not whether people can recognize right and wrong without believing in God.
This is the core formulation of Craig's moral case and separates moral ontology from moral knowledge, answering a recurring line of Hitchens's criticism.
Hitchens's portrayal of religious morality as humans needing divine commands in order to identify and perform right actions.
Craig argues that an evolutionary account may explain moral sentiments but cannot by itself furnish the objective grounding for duties both debaters wish to affirm.
Even if miracles or suspensions of natural law occur, they do not establish the truth of the miracle worker's doctrine or divine identity.
The argument attacks the inferential link between reported supernatural acts and Christian truth, bearing directly on Craig's appeal to Jesus's authority.
Craig's claim that Jesus's miracle working and exorcisms illustrate an unprecedented divine authority.
Using the scriptural example of Pharaoh's miracle-working magicians, Hitchens argues that miraculous performance alone cannot authenticate the performer's theological teaching.
Hitchens has offered no positive argument for God's nonexistence, while God's general revelation and just judgment address people outside Christian history.
Craig combines his burden-of-proof challenge with a substantive reply to the objection that most humans lived before or beyond access to Christianity.
Hitchens's defense of atheism and his objection that divine concern appears absent across most of humanity's history.
Opening his response, Craig says positive atheism remains unsupported and argues that pre-Christian and unevangelized people receive general revelation and are judged justly on what they know.
The universe's origin and fine-tuning support a personal creator and designer because Hitchens has not defeated the relevant premises or evidence.
Cosmological origin and fine-tuning are two of Craig's principal affirmative reasons for the debate's central conclusion that Christian theism is rationally supported.
Hitchens's earlier objections to design and his characterization of the universe as moving toward nothingness.
Craig says the cosmological premises went unchallenged and maintains that established fine-tuning survives Hitchens's objection because cosmic decline assumes rather than disproves atheism.
Without God, evolutionary and cultural accounts yield moral conventions rather than objective duties, whereas theism supplies a transcendent moral foundation.
Objective morality is one of Craig's principal affirmative arguments, and this passage directly answers Hitchens while explaining the alleged inadequacy of naturalism.
Hitchens's demand for a uniquely religious moral action and his focus on whether believers behave better than unbelievers.
Craig distinguishes grounding from behavior, argues that atheism cannot condemn competing social ethics objectively, and uses naturalistic accounts of morality to illustrate conventionalism.
The disciples' radically un-Jewish resurrection belief is best explained by the empty tomb and postmortem appearances of Jesus.
The resurrection is Craig's principal specifically Christian argument and is necessary to move his case from generic theism toward Christian theism.
Hitchens's treatment of the resurrection argument as an inference from Christianity's success or from an improbable story.
Craig says the argument is not that religious success proves truth, but that the origin of the disciples' anomalous belief requires the empty tomb and appearances as its explanation.
Religious improbability and rapidly generated miracle rumors do not establish truth; Gospel miracle claims ultimately require an act of faith.
The move directly contests the historical reliability and explanatory force of miracle testimony, thereby challenging Craig's resurrection case and religious epistemology.
Craig's argument that the unusual origin of resurrection belief supports the empty tomb and postmortem appearances.
Hitchens rejects improbability as evidence, recounts a disputed modern healing claim to demonstrate rumor formation, and contrasts credulous testimony with properly attested evidence.
Treating religion as a human creation explains its plurality and failures, while abolishing it would leave ordinary ethical problems unchanged and permit greater freedom.
This passage consolidates Hitchens's alternative account of religion and his central claim that morality neither depends upon nor benefits from celestial authority.
Craig's claim that theism uniquely explains morality and provides an objective basis unavailable to atheistic naturalism.
After surveying religion's political record, Hitchens argues that human authorship explains competing faiths and that justice, love, duty, and evolved impulses remain human problems without religion.
Without God and an objective moral code, nature supplies no moral limits, whereas biblical sexual guidelines can promote human well-being rather than repression.
The move directly applies Craig's moral argument to the dispute over whether religious sexual rules are harmful repression or defensible moral guidance.
Hitchens's claim that biblical sexual prohibitions express repression, fear, and control rather than sound moral guidance.
Following Hitchens's answer about sexual repression, Craig argues that naturalism provides no objective restriction and that religious sexual guidance can benefit people.
Appealing to supernatural authority does not clarify sexual morality, because natural homosexuality conflicts with religious prohibition and circumcision was intended to diminish pleasure.
The move challenges the explanatory and moral value of divine sexual commands, directly contesting Craig's defense of religious guidance as beneficial.
Craig's contention that objective divine morality supplies beneficial sexual guidelines rather than harmful or repressive restrictions.
Hitchens counters Craig by arguing that homosexuality occurs naturally despite religious bans and that traditional explanations of circumcision reveal deliberate suppression of pleasure.
Religion's harmful record is relevant when scriptures themselves command atrocities, unlike scientific discoveries that can be used destructively without constituting an ideology.
This move states Hitchens's core record-of-religion argument in its strongest form: the evil is attributed to authoritative religious commands, not merely bad adherents.
The student's analogy between religious violence and the violence enabled by physicists through creation of the nuclear bomb.
Hitchens rejects the analogy between physics and religion, maintaining that scientific knowledge is not a belief system while religious texts can specifically enjoin mutilation and extermination.
A worldview's truth cannot be inferred from its beneficial or harmful social consequences, so the debate should turn on arguments for truth rather than comparative death tolls.
The move supplies a governing criterion for the debate and directly attempts to exclude a major line of Hitchens's case as irrelevant to whether theism is true.
The broader contention that Christianity or religion should be discredited because of its destructive historical and cultural consequences.
Craig declines to compare atrocities committed by atheists and Christians, invoking a two-way principle that neither good nor bad social effects establish a worldview's truth.
On atheism human existence can have subjective projects but no objective purpose, whereas fellowship with God provides humanity's true fulfillment and enduring meaning.
The move develops a principal existential argument for theism by grounding objective purpose in God and denying that temporary chosen projects can supply comparable meaning.
The audience challenge asking why an unbeliever's fulfilling and moral life should be considered absurd or purposeless without God.
Craig distinguishes serving God from enjoying fellowship with God, then argues that cosmic extinction under atheism makes all human purposes objectively meaningless despite subjective fulfillment.
Atheism honestly accepts unwelcome conclusions while human freedom and solidarity can make life meaningful without immortality, and religious power obstructs liberty in this world.
The move answers Craig's existential argument with a positive secular basis for meaning while connecting that basis to Hitchens's wider criticism of coercive religion.
Craig's assertion that atheism leaves human existence objectively meaningless and reduces personal purposes to subjective illusions.
Hitchens treats acceptance of mortality as evidential honesty, locates meaning in struggles for freedom and solidarity, and argues that purported divine authority threatens those values.
Neither the logical nor probabilistic problem of evil defeats theism, and Christianity addresses suffering through God's sufficient reasons, Christ's suffering, and hope of eternal life.
The move directly answers one of the motion's principal issues by addressing both intellectual arguments from evil and the emotional force of experienced suffering.
The Epicurean challenge that an omniscient, omnipotent, and perfectly good God would intervene to prevent severe innocent suffering.
Craig separates logical, probabilistic, and emotional problems of evil, argues that atheists cannot exclude divine reasons for suffering, and presents the cross as Christianity's existential answer.
Theism can render any horror compatible with divine purpose, as illustrated by unanswered suffering whose later compensation would make an abuser an instrument of God's will.
The move targets the unfalsifiability and moral cost of the theistic response to suffering by showing how promised compensation can absorb even extreme abuse into providence.
Craig's argument that God may have morally sufficient reasons for permitting suffering and can ultimately redeem it through salvation and eternal life.
Hitchens partly concedes that theism can accommodate suffering, then argues that this very flexibility turns prolonged unanswered agony into something deemed worthwhile within divine providence.
Public interest in debates about God reflects both the urgent worldwide danger of theocratic movements and a growing willingness to confront religious bullying through open argument.
The move synthesizes Hitchens's practical case against religion by connecting contemporary theocratic threats with the need for public scrutiny of religious claims.
Hitchens attributes renewed attention to religion to theocratic violence and coercion across several traditions, alongside a small movement committed to challenging such claims publicly.
Renewed interest in God reflects disillusionment with naturalistic modernity's meaninglessness and a philosophical revival that is reestablishing the intellectual credibility of theism.
The move closes Craig's case by framing naturalism as existentially barren and presenting contemporary philosophical theism as a rational alternative gaining wider influence.
Hitchens's explanation that interest in religious debate primarily arises from dangerous theocratic movements and organized resistance to their bullying.
Craig interprets the debate's popularity as a reaction against the failed humanistic promise of modernity and as the public diffusion of a major renaissance in Christian philosophy.
